name: Tsuvadi
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Tsuvaɗi exhibits two level tones in its lexicon: High (H), Low (L), and one contour High-Low, or High-Falling (HL). All three can be observed in nouns with the noun class prefix hAC-, which consistently bears high tone [...] Phonetically, the Low tone can be realized as a level or—more frequently at the end of words—a low falling pitch. However, the falling pitch starting at Low tone is considered an allotone (phonetic variant) of Low. [p. 63] [...] In Tsuvaɗi, all verbs exhibit grammatical tone and are lexically toneless. For disyllabic verb roots in the Realis mood, the verb takes a L-H.L melody on the index and root. In the Irrealis mood, the verb takes a H-L.HL melody on the index and root. [p. 73]
new_statements.citation: Buttacavoli, Ryan. 2022. A Phonological Sketch of the Tsuvaɗi Language with a Focus on the Tsudugu Dialect. Jos: SIL Nigeria (SIL Language & Culture Archives 93494), 77 pp.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 5.1 Lexical Tone, p. 63 (PDF p. 63); sec. 5.2 Grammatical Tone, p. 73 (PDF p. 73)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tsuvaɗi is described as a tone language with two level tones (H, L) and an HL contour on nouns, automatic downdrift, and grammatical (mood-driven) tone melodies on lexically toneless verbs. Neither Buttacavoli 2022 nor Blench 2007 (sec. 3.3 Tones, p. 5: 'high, low and falling') mentions stress, accent or prominence at all, so no word-stress position can be assigned; the language is tonal per both sources and silent on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none discussed). Tone: HL on the noun-class prefix is rare (p. 70); word-final L takes a falling allotone in isolation (p. 63).
new_statements.domain_note: Words elicited in isolation from a ~2000-item recorded wordlist (citation forms); nouns = class prefix + root, 2-4 syllables (p. 53). No phrase-level prosody beyond downdrift in associative constructions (p. 72).
new_statements.identity_note: Buttacavoli 2022 describes the Tsudugu (Adugu) dialect, the Bible-translation target lect (data from Momo, Azhezhaha, Udara, Tudun Muntsira, Idaci villages); Glottolog gives Tsudugu no separate glottocode (its record reads 'Tsugudu = Tsuvadi [tvd]'), and the SIL survey's two named dialects are Tsuvaɗi-Agaɗi (Azagaɗi, east) and Tsuvaɗi-Azozolo (west). Blench 2007 is based on a 1999 session at Ragara plus David Lovelace's 1990 lexical data (dialect unspecified). Both fall under tsuv1239; no dialect-level glottocode exists.

sources.note: Nothing: the words stress/accent/prominence do not occur in the 77-page text layer. Ch. 4 Syllable Structure (pp. 50-62) and ch. 5 Tones (pp. 63-75): two level tones H, L plus HL contour on nouns (p. 63); verbs lexically toneless with grammatical tone melodies (p. 73); downdrift, falling allotone of L at word end.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic only; identifies two Tsuvaɗi dialects (Tsuvaɗi-Agaɗi, Tsuvaɗi-Azozolo); previous-research paragraph names Lovelace 1990 1800-item wordlist and Camburn 1999. Nothing on stress or tone.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 3.3 Tones (p. 5): 'high, low and falling... This also seems to be the system of TsuVaɗi'; 'The tone of nominal prefixes is driven by the stem in all cases, while the tones of verbs seem to reflect the numbers of syllables.'
